# Riding Shoes

> **Biography of Dongfang Shuo**: Emperor Wu said to Shuo, "I wish to make my beloved favorites never grow old. Is that possible?" Shuo replied, "I can do it." The Emperor asked, "What medicine should be taken?" He answered, "In the northeast there is a spirit mushroom <term>zhicao</term> <gloss>lingzhi, a plant of immortality</gloss>. When I was a child, someone led me to go gather this herb, but we were blocked by the Red Spring and could not cross. That man gave me one of his shoes, and I then went upstream along the spring, obtained it, and ate it."

## Riding Shoes

> **Biography of Dongfang Shuo** <note>From the *Hanshu* (Book of Han)</note>: Emperor Wu said to Dongfang Shuo: "I wish to make those I love and favor never grow old. Is this possible?" Shuo replied: "Your servant can accomplish this." The Emperor said: "What medicine should one take?" He replied: "In the northeastern lands there grows a lingzhi mushroom. When I was a child, someone led me there to gather this herb, but we were separated by the Red Spring and could not cross. That person gave me a single shoe, and I was then able to ford the spring, obtain the mushroom, and eat it."

# Volume 40

**Wine Offerings.** At the principal and accompanying positions, the Grand Vessel <note>太尊, the largest ceremonial wine vessel</note> is filled with <term>fan qi</term> <gloss>thin ritual wine with floating sediment</gloss> and <term>li qi</term> <gloss>sweet ritual wine</gloss>. The Standing Vessel <note>著尊</note> is filled with <term>ang qi</term> <gloss>clear ritual wine</gloss>. The Sacrificial Vessel <note>犧尊, often decorated with animal motifs</note> is filled with <term>ti qi</term> <gloss>reddish ritual wine</gloss>. The Mountain Ewer <note>山罍, a large vessel decorated with mountain patterns</note> is filled with aged wine. These are placed upon the altar. The Grand Vessel is filled with <term>chen qi</term> <gloss>precipitated ritual wine</gloss>, and the Mountain Ewer is filled with service wine and clear wine. These are placed below the altar. For the subordinate positions, the Standing Vessel is filled with <term>li qi</term> <gloss>sweet ritual wine</gloss> and <term>ang qi</term> <gloss>clear ritual wine</gloss>, and the Sacrificial Vessel is filled with service wine.

**Grain Offerings.** At the principal position, the accompanying position, and the subordinate positions, the <term>fu</term> <gloss>square ritual grain vessels</gloss> are filled with broomcorn millet and common millet, and the <term>gui</term> <gloss>round ritual grain vessels</gloss> are filled with rice and fine millet.

**Contents of the Bamboo Trays and Wooden Dishes.** At the Square Mound, for the principal and accompanying positions, each bamboo tray <note>籩, used for dry offerings</note> is filled with: salt and dried fish, jujubes, chestnuts, hazelnuts, water caltrop, gorgon fruit, dried deer meat, dark cakes, white cakes, parched grain cakes, and rice flour cakes. Each wooden dish <note>豆, used for moist offerings</note> is filled with: pickled chives, meat paste, pickled turnip greens, deer meat paste, pickled celery, rabbit meat paste, pickled bamboo shoots, fish paste, pickled tripe, pressed pork, filled food, and mixed grain food. For the subordinate positions, the bamboo trays omit the parched grain cakes and rice flour cakes, and the wooden dishes omit the filled food and mixed grain food.

The cushion positions use crimson fabric, following the same standard as the Suburban Heaven Sacrifice. The carriages and banners follow the same standard as the Heaven Sacrifice.

<summary>This page specifies the ritual wine vessels, grain offerings, and food arrangements for the Square Mound (Earth Altar) sacrifice, detailing which vessels hold which types of wine at the principal, accompanying, and subordinate positions, and listing the exact contents of bamboo trays and wooden dishes.</summary>

affairs; its Great Martial music represents King Wu's affairs. Both are called <term>xiang</term> <gloss>representation, image; here referring to a dance-music piece that "represents" a historical event</gloss>. However, the author of the preface here says "perform the Great Martial" and "Xiang dance"; in the "Wu" chapter one cannot again say "perform Xiang," so he simply points to the music's name and says "perform the Great Martial." In fact, the Great Martial music is also called Xiang. Therefore the <term>Liji</term> <gloss>Book of Rites</gloss>, in the chapters "King Wen as Heir," "Positions in the Ming Hall," and "Summary of Sacrifices," all state: "Ascend and sing <term>Qing Miao</term> <gloss>Pure Temple, a hymn in the Zhou Odes</gloss>; below, play <term>Xiang</term>." Xiang and Qing Miao are set in parallel, and both are poem titles. Therefore the commentary on "Positions in the Ming Hall" says that Xiang refers to the "Wu" poem in the Zhou Odes. Calling the Wu poem "Xiang" makes clear that the Great Martial chapter is also Xiang. However, the text of the Record, below the word "pipes," separately says "dance the Great Martial," meaning that the music of the Wu poem is also Xiang.

# 欽定四庫全書 · Imperially Approved Complete Library of the Four Treasuries

## [Chapter] One Hundred, first part

...it would certainly not be practiced. That former scholars held this view had, in fact, a genuine origin. The *Zuo Tradition* says: "Seven tones were established to serve the five notes." The *Discourses of Zhou* records that when King Wu attacked Shang, the year star was in <term>Chunhuo</term> <gloss>Quail Fire, a zodiacal region</gloss>, the moon was in <term>Tiansi</term> <gloss>Heavenly Steed</gloss>, the sun was at the ford of <term>Ximu</term> <gloss>Firewood Section</gloss>, the hour-marker was at the handle of the Dipper, and the stars were in <term>Tianyuan</term> <gloss>Heavenly Turtle</gloss>. From Quail Fire to the Heavenly Steed are the seven divisions of the heavens, spanning north and south as seven harmonies. The *Discourses of Chu* recounts that the sacrifices of the former kings had seven items, corresponding to heaven, earth, the people, and the labors of the four seasons. The *Great Tradition of the Documents* recounts that the sage kings made a tour of the twelve provinces and reviewed the customs of the twelve regions so as to establish the <term>qishi</term> <gloss>Seven Beginnings</gloss>, taking the seven as their framework. Scholars of the Han such as Jiao Yanshou, Jing Fang, and Zheng Kangcheng held that <term>Huangzhong</term> <gloss>Yellow Bell</gloss> is the gong note, <term>Taicu</term> <gloss>Great Pinch</gloss> the shang, <term>Guxian</term> <gloss>Jade Wash</gloss> the jue, <term>Linzhong</term> <gloss>Forest Bell</gloss> the zhi, <term>Nanlü</term> <gloss>Southern Pitch-pipe</gloss> the yu, <term>Yingzhong</term> <gloss>Responsive Bell</gloss> the altered gong, and <term>Ruibin</term> <gloss>Bushy Guest</gloss> the altered zhi: this is what is called the Seven Beginnings. Ban Gu further elaborated on this...

<summary>This page traces the origins of the seven-tone (qiyin) system, citing the Zuo Tradition, Discourses of Zhou and Chu, and the Documents' Great Tradition, and presenting the Han scholars Jiao Yanshou, Jing Fang, Zheng Kangcheng, and Ban Gu, who mapped the seven notes onto the twelve pitch-standards as the Seven Beginnings.</summary>
<keywords>seven tones, seven beginnings, five notes, Zuo Tradition, Discourses of Zhou, King Wu, pitch-standards, Huangzhong, altered gong, altered zhi, Jiao Yanshou, Jing Fang, Zheng Kangcheng, Ban Gu, Chen Yang, Yue Shu</keywords>

<margin>Imperially Commissioned Complete Library of the Four Treasuries: *Mao Shi Zhushu* <gloss>Commentaries and Subcommentaries on the Mao Odes</gloss>, page 13</margin>

...the matter of it. The music of the *Da Wu* <gloss>Great Wu, the dance depicting King Wu's deeds</gloss> represents the deeds of King Wu. The two are both forms of *xiang* <gloss>representational dance</gloss>, but in the Preface, at this point it says "they performed the *Da Wu*, the *xiang* dance," and within the piece "Wu" one could not again speak of performing the *xiang*; therefore it names the music itself, saying "they performed the *Da Wu*." In reality the music of the *Da Wu* is also a *xiang*. Therefore in the *Book of Rites*, in "King Wen's Heir," "The Mingtang Position," and "A Summary Account of Sacrifices," it is everywhere said: "They ascended and sang the *Qing Miao* <gloss>Pure Temple, an ode of the Zhou</gloss>, and below performed the *guan* pipes with the *xiang*." Since the *xiang* and the *Qing Miao* are paired together, both are poem pieces. Therefore the commentary on "The Mingtang Position" says the *xiang* refers to the "Wu" of the Zhou Hymns <gloss>the Wu section of the *Zhou Song*</gloss>. To call the poem "Wu" a *xiang* makes clear that the piece *Da Wu* is also a *xiang*. But the text of the Rites, after the pipes, separately says "they danced the *Da Wu*," saying that the music of the poem "Wu" is likewise a *xiang*...

The Kong commentary<note>Kong Yingda's sub-commentary (Shu)</note>: In the twentieth year of Duke Zhao, Yan Ying said <gloss>a single sound from the qin or se zithers cannot make music</gloss>. Fang means pattern and adornment. The gan is a shield; the qi is an axe.

These are what the martial dance holds. The yu is the feather of the di pheasant; the mao is the tail of the mao ox. These are what the civil dance holds. In the Rites of Zhou, the dance master and music master are in charge of teaching the dances: there is a weapons dance, a shield dance, a feather dance, and an ox-tail dance. <gloss>Kong notes that the Rites of Zhou contain a shield dance but no weapons dance; Zheng, the Grand Minister of Agriculture, says the shield dance is the weapons dance; Zheng cites the Music</gloss> and adds the weapons dance, because the text says "shield and axe," which refers to the Grand Wu dance. <gloss>The Odes say: "In the left hand he holds the yue flute, in the right he grasps the di feathers"</gloss> <gloss>Kong cites this to prove that the feather dance is the dance with di feathers</gloss>. Kong Yingda says: this chapter discusses how music arises from the human heart, and therefore is named "music." The human heart, once moved by external things, expresses the heart through the mouth, and the heart's form appears in sound. If the heart is stirred by things of death and mourning and this stirs the mouth, then it appears in sounds of grief. If the heart is stirred by blessings and celebrations and this stirs the mouth, then it appears in

# Volume Forty

**Wine and beverage offerings.** At the principal and paired positions<note>the tablets of the chief deity and accompanying deities</note> the Grand Zun vessels<note><term>taizun</term> <gloss>largest wine vessel type</gloss></note> are filled with Fanqi wine<note><term>fanqi</term> <gloss>a lightly fermented, foamy wine</gloss></note>, the Zhuzun vessels<note><term>zhuzun</term> <gloss>a plain-bodied wine vessel</gloss></note> with Angqi wine<note><term>angqi</term> <gloss>a clearer, more fermented wine</gloss></note>, the Xi Zun vessels<note><term>xizun</term> <gloss>vessels decorated with sacrificial ox motifs</gloss></note> with Tiqi wine<note><term>tiqi</term> <gloss>a red, well-fermented wine</gloss></note>, and the Shanlei vessels<note><term>shanlei</term> <gloss>lei wine jars carved with mountain designs</gloss></note> with Xijiu wine<note><term>xijiu</term> <gloss>aged wine from the previous year</gloss></note>; these stand upon the mound altar. Below the altar, the Grand Zun are filled with Chenqi wine<note><term>chenqi</term> <gloss>clarified wine settled of its lees</gloss></note>, and the Shanlei vessels with Shijiu<note><term>shijiu</term> <gloss>wine brewed for the occasion</gloss></note> and Qingjiu<note><term>qingjiu</term> <gloss>fully clarified wine</gloss></note>. At the accompanying positions<note>for the secondary deities in attendance</note>, the Zhuzun vessels hold Liqi wine<note><term>liqi</term> <gloss>sweet, unstrained rice wine</gloss></note> and Angqi wine, and the Xi Zun vessels hold Shijiu wine.

**Grain offerings.**** At the principal, paired, and accompanying positions alike, the Fu vessels<note><term>fu</term> <gloss>square grain vessels</gloss></note> are filled with millet and broomcorn millet, and the Gui vessels<note><term>gui</term> <gloss>round grain vessels</gloss></note> with rice and fine grain.

**Contents of the Bian and Dou vessels.** At the Square Mound<note><term>fangqiu</term> <gloss>the Earth Altar, square in shape, matching heaven's round altar</gloss></note> for the principal and paired positions, each Bian basket<note><term>bian</term> <gloss>shallow bamboo food basket</gloss></note> holds salt, dried fish, dates, chestnuts, hazelnuts, water chestnuts, gorgon fruit, dried venison, black cakes, white cakes, and Qier made from roasted grain flour<note><term>qier</term> <gloss>sweetmeats of parched grain and honey</gloss></note> and Fenchyi<note><term>fenchyi</term> <gloss>rice-paste cakes fried in oil</gloss></note>. Each Dou dish<note><term>dou</term> <gloss>stemmed food dish</gloss></note> holds pickled chives, minced pickled meat sauce, pickled cress, venison sauce, pickled celery, rabbit sauce, pickled bamboo shoots, fish sauce, pickled ox-spleen<note><term>pixi</term> <gloss>a dish of sliced spleen or offal in pickle</gloss></note>, pressed pork slices, Bao dishes of boiled meat, and Shenshi dumplings of seasoned rice and meat<note><term>shenshi</term> <gloss>a dish of rice kneaded with minced meat</gloss></note>. For the accompanying positions, the Bian baskets are without the Qier and Fenchyi cakes, and the Dou dishes are without the Bao and Shenshi offerings.

**Carpet positions.** These use crimson silk, the same as in the sacrifice to Heaven at the suburb altar.

**Chariots and banners.** These are the same as in the sacrifice to Heaven.

<summary>This page details the ceremonial offerings at the Square Mound (Earth Altar): the graded quality of wine in various ritual vessels at principal, paired, and accompanying positions, the grain offerings in square and round vessels, the full list of foods in the bian baskets and dou dishes, and notes that carpeting and banners follow the rites of the Heaven sacrifice.</summary>
<keywords>Square Mound, Earth Altar, ritual vessels, zun, lei, wine offerings, grain offerings, fu, gui, bian, dou, Fangqiu, sacrifice to Earth, Qin Ding Li Qi Tu Shi</keywords>

On those days, the workers were customarily led into their positions; when the <term>xielülang</term> <gloss>music supervisor, the court official who directed the orchestra by raising and lowering a banner</gloss> raised the banner, the music began; when he lowered it, the music ceased. The civil dance withdrew and the martial dance advanced: this was the established practice.

After the An Lushan rebellion of the <term>Tianbao</term> <gloss>Heavenly Treasure, 742–756, the era name marking the catastrophe</gloss> era, Emperor Suzong reconquered the two capitals <note>Chang'an and Luoyang</note>. From the <term>Zhide</term> <gloss>era name, 756–758</gloss> period onward, the palace-scale orchestra <term>gongjia</term> <gloss>the full court instrumental arrangement set on frames around the courtyard</gloss> was set up only for the New Year's audience of congratulation at Hanyuan Hall; for all other sacrifices at the suburban altars and ancestral temple there was only the terrace song <term>dengge</term> <gloss>vocal hymns performed on the raised terrace, without instrumental accompaniment below</gloss>, and no music or dancing in the courtyard beneath the altar.

After the <term>Guangming</term> <gloss>era name of Xizong, 880–881, when Huang Chao's forces took the capital</gloss> disturbances under Emperor Xizong, the golden notes <note>the bronze-bell and stone-chime music</note> had all but perished, and a search for recruits and for the instruments of the frames found scarcely any that survived. When Emperor Zhaozong was about to perform the sacrifices at the suburban altars and ancestral temple, the officials petitioned to have the frame-music constructed anew. Thereupon the chief minister Zhang Jun was made Commissioner for Building and Restoring the Instruments and Frames, and gathered all the craftsmen of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices <term>Taichang</term> <gloss>the state office in charge of rituals and music</gloss> to inquire into it; but they could not attain the old method. The erudite scholar Shang Yingsun, versed in the ancient records, took his model from the <term>shunju</term> <gloss>the wooden frames on which chimes and bells were suspended</gloss>, and in casting bells determined their weight and height accordingly; he then fixed the Pitch-perfect bells by cross-checking them, establishing the Yellow Bell <term>Huangzhong</term> <gloss>the fundamental pitch of the twelve-tone Chinese system</gloss> at nine cun and five fen, and the doubled Response Bell <term>Yingzhong</term> <gloss>the twelfth pitch, an octave above the Yellow Bell</gloss>...

<summary>A history of ritual music after the An Lushan rebellion: the decline of the full palace orchestra from Suzong's reign through the chaos under Xizong, and Zhaozong's late-Tang attempt to rebuild it under minister Zhang Jun with the music scholar Shang Yingsun rederiving the bell standards.</summary>
<keywords>xielülang music supervisor, civil and martial dances, An Lushan rebellion, Suzong, Hanyuan Hall, gongjia palace orchestra, dengge terrace song, Xizong, Guangming era, Zhaozong, Zhang Jun, Taichang, Shang Yingsun, shunju bell frames, Huangzhong Yellow Bell, Yingzhong Response Bell</keywords>

# The Master said: "If this is not the sound of Wu, then what sound is it?" The reply was: "The officials have lost the transmission. If it is not that the officials have lost the transmission, then King Wu's ambition has grown senile."

<gloss>The "officials" refers to those in charge of music. "Transmission" here means the explanation or teaching. "Senile" means old and feeble-minded. This states that the music officials lost their proper explanation, and people of the time made erroneous claims.</gloss>

# The Master said: "Indeed. I, Qiu, have heard from Chang Hong words that also match what you say."

<gloss>Chang Hong was a grand master of the Zhou dynasty. The commentary notes the concern that he may not have lived to witness these events directly, suggesting that Chang Hong expanded upon earlier accounts. The "prolonged and drawn-out singing" mentioned refers to the style of vocal performance in the Wu dance.</gloss>

The dance represents King Wu's campaign against Zhou, the last ruler of the Shang dynasty. Fearing that the feudal lords would not arrive in time, and that the military campaign would not advance, the singing voice is prolonged, drawn out, and scattered in its beauty. This answer is correct.

At the beginning of the dance, the hands and feet are raised high, stamping the ground with fierce and vigorous movement. At the opening of the dance it is indeed so, and therefore it is said to be premature. When it comes to the timely affair, this refers to King Wu's timely campaign against Zhou and the battle that followed. Therefore the vigorous, stamping movements represent warfare. This answer is not correct. We know it is not correct because the text below states that "the vigorous stamping and fierce movements" express the ambition of a great man. Therefore we know this answer is wrong.

"Expressing one's will" means rising up with determination. The question asks: why does the martial man suddenly sometimes kneel? With the right knee reaching the ground while the left foot is raised upward, what is the reason for this? The reply states: "This is not the sitting posture of Wu." This means attacking to the right and cutting to the left; it is not the sitting posture of a martial man. It states that in this dance method there is no sitting at all. This answer is also incorrect. We know it is incorrect from what follows below.

This was King Wu's accomplishment, and so the Duke of Zhou created music, taking the *Dawu* <gloss>Great martial dance</gloss> as King Wu's music. According to the *Record of Music* <note>original: "樂記"</note>, it says: "King Wu's [music] made manifest the achievement." <gloss>The commentary says: this is the name of Yao's music; the *Rites of Zhou* omits it, or it appears as *Da Juan*</gloss> It further says: "*Xianchi* is complete." <gloss>The commentary says: this is the name of music made by the Yellow Emperor, who augmented it and put it to use</gloss> The *Rites of Zhou* calls it *Da Xian* <gloss>Great Xian</gloss>, which differs from the names of the pieces in this text and its commentary. The origin is that the Yellow Emperor's music was named *Xianchi*. Because the Five Emperors lived in different eras and did not perpetuate one another's music, if Yao augmented the body of the Yellow Emperor's music while preserving its original name, it was still called *Xianchi*, and this is what the *Da Xian* <gloss>Great Xian</gloss> refers to. But if the musical form remained unchanged without augmentation, then the original name was changed and it was called *Da Zhang* <gloss>Great Pattern</gloss>, hence the statement that *Da Zhang* is Yao's music. When the Duke of Zhou created the music, he further made *Da Juan* <gloss>Great Circle</gloss>. *Da Juan* is the same as *Da Zhang*. Though *Da Zhang* is the name of Yao's music, its substance is the Yellow Emperor's music; therefore this *Da Juan* is also counted as the Yellow Emperor's music. Since, in Yao's time, the preserved Yellow Emperor music *Xianchi* bore the name of Yao's music, the Duke of Zhou instead gave the Yellow Emperor's music a new name, *Yunmen* <gloss>Cloud Gate</gloss>, making it one with *Da Juan*. This is why, later in the text under "apportioning the music and setting it in order," *Da Juan* is not listed separately. That music names were indeed changed <gloss>one account says this</gloss> can be seen from the *Xiu-tie lun* <note>possibly a lost treatise; the reading is uncertain</note>, which says: Ban Gu composed the *Book of Han*; in the fourth year of Gaozu [of Han], the music *Wude* <gloss>Martial Virtue</gloss> was created. It further says that in the temple of Gaozu, *Wude* and *Wenshi* were performed. <gloss>The commentary says: *Wenshi* was the name of Shun's *Shao* dance; it was performed under the First Emperor of Qin</gloss> In the twenty-sixth year, it was renamed the *Wuxing* dance <gloss>Five Phases dance</gloss>. <gloss>The commentary says: *Wuxing* was originally the dance of Zhou; it was renamed in the sixth year of Gaozu</gloss> to the *Wenshi Wuxing* dance. From this we know there was a practice of changing music names. According to the *Weft of the Classic of Filial Piety* <note>original: "孝經緯"; a Han apocryphal text</note>: Fuxi's music was called *Liji* <gloss>Establishing the Foundation</gloss>; Shennong's music was called *Xiamou* <gloss>Lower Planning</gloss>; and Zhurong's music was called *Zhuxu* <gloss>Continuing Succession</gloss>.

This is because King Wu achieved his success, and so the Duke of Zhou composed music, establishing "Da Wu" <gloss>Great Martial</gloss> as King Wu's music. According to the *Record of Music*, "King Wu's chapter" means to make it manifest. <gloss>The note says: This is the name of Yao's music. The *Zhou Li* omits it; some read it as "Da Juan" (Great Scroll).</gloss> It also says: "Xian Chi <gloss>Salinity Pool</gloss> is complete." <gloss>The note says: This is the name of music composed by the Yellow Emperor. The Yellow Emperor expanded and refined it, and used it.</gloss>

The *Zhou Li* calls it "Da Xian" <gloss>Great Salinity</gloss>, which differs from the music names given in this classic's commentary. The reason is this: originally the Yellow Emperor's music was called "Xian Chi." Because the Five Emperors ruled in different eras and did not inherit one another's music, if Yao expanded and refined the body of the Yellow Emperor's music, he preserved its original name and still called it "Xian Chi," which is this "Da Xian." But if the body of the music remained unchanged and was not expanded, then he altered the original name and called it "Da Zhang" <gloss>Great Display</gloss>. Hence it is said: "Da Zhang is Yao's music."

When the Duke of Zhou composed music, he further created "Da Juan" <gloss>Great Scroll</gloss>. Da Juan is the same as Da Zhang. Although Da Zhang is the name of Yao's music, its substance is the Yellow Emperor's music, and so this Da Juan is also, in one sense, the Yellow Emperor's music. The Duke of Zhou, since in Yao's time the Yellow Emperor's Xian Chi had been preserved as the name of Yao's music, then established a new name for the Yellow Emperor's music, calling it "Yun Men" <gloss>Cloud Gate</gloss>, making it one with Da Juan. Therefore, when the text below distributes and arranges the music in sequence, it does not separately list Da Juan again.

That one may be certain there existed the practice of renaming music <gloss>one reading says: "of changing"</gloss>, we may examine the *Xiudie Lun* <note>a lost work on ritual discussion</note>, which states: Ban Gu, composing the *Book of Han*, records that in the fourth year of Emperor Gaozu, the music of "Wu De" <gloss>Martial Virtue</gloss> was composed. It also says: In the temple of Emperor Gaozu, they performed "Wu De" and "Wen Shi." <gloss>The note says: Wen Shi is the name of Shun's Shao dance; it was performed beginning with the First Emperor.</gloss> In the twenty-sixth year, it was renamed the "Wu Xing" <gloss>Five Phases</gloss> dance. <gloss>The note says: Wu Xing was originally the Zhou dance; in the sixth year of Emperor Gaozu it was renamed.</gloss> It was called the dance of Wen Shi and Wu Xing. From this we know that there existed a tradition of renaming music.

According to the *Xiao Jing Wei* <gloss>Apocryphal Classic of Filial Piety</gloss>: Fuxi's music was called "Li Ji" <gloss>Establishing the Foundation</gloss>; Shennong's music was called "Xia Mou" <gloss>Descending Plan</gloss>; Zhurong's music was called "Shu Xu" <gloss>Continuing the Sequence</gloss>.

# After the "Ba Yi" and "Yong Che" passages, it is suspected to have been spoken against those who usurped rites and music.
<gloss>Master Li, given name Yu, courtesy name Guangzu, a man of Zhaowu</gloss>

○ From the Recorded Sayings: Master You spoke of the heart-mind, Master Cheng spoke of principle, and Master Li spoke of the human person. Each of these addresses the idea that the Way does not travel of itself without a person to carry it. The heart-mind contains this principle; preserving the heart-mind, however, depends on the human being. Humaneness is the complete virtue of the original heart. If a person preserves the original, innate good heart without losing it, then what he does will naturally have order and harmony. But once this heart is lost, only selfish desires and private aims come out of him; how could there be order and harmony? Humaneness is simply principle, the pattern of what ought to be, and principle must reside within the human heart before one can properly speak of the word "humaneness" in its fullness. ○ Master Rao said: Master You's explanation grasps the word "humaneness" directly and intimately, but the two words "rites and music" are not clearly distinguished. Master Cheng's explanation of the two words "rites and music" is meaningful, but the word "humaneness" is not so intimate. One must combine the two explanations into one before the meaning of humaneness together with rites and music is complete. Master Cheng's "no order, no harmony" describes the case of rites and music lacking their substance; Master Li's "bells, drums, jade, and silk" describes the case of rites and music having their outward forms. These two explanations, too, must be combined into one before the meaning of "what can one do about rites and music?" is fully exhausted. The Collected Commentary uses its meaning with great subtlety and depth; it requires careful reading. Master You said that rites and music are spoken of in terms of their substance and function, while Master Cheng spoke only of rites and music in themselves.

Every five years a grand sacrifice <term>yin ji</term> <gloss>a great, combined ancestral sacrifice</gloss> is performed.

Under the old Han regulations, every three years a *di* sacrifice was held: the tablets of destroyed temples were gathered to feast at the temple of Gaozu <note>Gaozu, founder of the Han dynasty</note>, while the tablets of temples still in existence had never been brought together for joint sacrifice. In the fifth year of the Yuanshi era <note>A.D. 5</note>, the *di* sacrifice was first instituted in this form. And again, eighteen years earlier, the emperor had personally gone to Chang'an and performed this same rite. The word *di* means "to settle" <note>original: 諦; a play on words, *di* 禘 and *di* 諦</note>: it settles and fixes the meaning of precedence between the generations, the *zhaomu* order of honor and rank <term>zhaomu</term> <gloss>the alternating generation labels (zhao and mu) that determine ancestral tablet placement</gloss>. The *di* sacrifice is held in the fourth month of summer. Summer is when the yang vapors are above and the yin vapors are below; hence it corrects the principle of superior and inferior rank. The *sha* <gloss>combined sacrifice</gloss> is held in the tenth month of winter. Winter is when the five grains are ripe and all things are complete, the rites fulfilled; hence all are gathered together for food and drink. This institution has now lapsed for eight years; it is requested that it be carried out in accordance with the rites, in due season.

The *Baihu Tong* <gloss>Comprehensive Discussions in the White Tiger Hall, a Han Confucian classic</gloss>: In the *di* sacrifice, the tablets of all the destroyed temples join in feast at the temple of the First Ancestor.

According to the *Wujing Tongyi* <gloss>Comprehensive Meanings of the Five Classics</gloss>: For kings and feudal lords, three years bring one intercalary month, and the Way of Heaven is then slightly complete; hence every three years there is one *sha*. In the *sha*, the tablets of all temples not yet relocated are taken and joined in feast in the temple of the First Ancestor. Five years bring a second intercalation, and the Way of Heaven is then greatly complete; hence every five years there is one *di*. In the *di*, the tablets of temples already relocated are taken and joined in feast in the temple, for one must not forget the persons of the former ancestors: their line of descent is maintained, from the near to the distant, and the former ancestors are not forgotten.

# Imperially Commissioned Complete Library of the Four Treasuries: Volume 170 of the Imperially Commissioned Yuanjian Leihan <note>御定淵鑑類函卷一百七十</note>

The spirit tablets from both dismantled temples and temples not yet dismantled all ascend to share in the combined feast at the Grand Ancestor's temple. <note>The "dismantled temples" (毀廟) refer to ancestral shrines of more distant forebears whose tablets have been removed from active worship due to generational distance. "Combined feast" (合食) means all ancestral spirits are gathered together to receive offerings simultaneously.</note> Every five years there are two grand sacrifices. <note>The term 殷祭 (yīn jì), "grand sacrifice," refers to the two major collective ancestral rites held within each five-year cycle: one xiá (祫) and one dì (禘).</note>

Under the old Han system, a dì sacrifice was held every three years. Tablets from dismantled temples were brought to share in the combined feast at the High Temple, but tablets from extant temples were not included in the combined sacrifice. In the fifth year of Yuanshi <note>5 CE, during the reign of Wang Mang's regency</note>, the dì sacrifice was performed for the first time. Also, eighteen years earlier, the emperor had personally traveled to Chang'an and performed this same rite there.

The word dì (禘) means "to examine and determine" (諦). <note>This is a phonetic gloss (聲訓), explaining the ritual term through a homophone: 禘 is glossed by 諦, meaning "to scrutinize" or "to ascertain."</note> It signifies the establishment of the proper order of seniority in the alternating generational arrangement. <note>The zhāo-mù (昭穆) system arranges ancestral tablets in alternating rows: even-numbered generations face one direction, odd-numbered generations face the other, so that the relative positions of ancestors are clearly fixed.</note> The dì sacrifice is held in the fourth month of summer because in summer the yang qi is above and the yin qi is below, and thus the principle of fixing seniority is made manifest. The dì sacrifice is also held in the tenth month of winter because in winter the five grains have ripened and all things are complete, and so the ancestors are gathered together for a communal feast. This canonical rite has fallen into disuse for eight years now. It is respectfully requested that it be carried out in accordance with ritual at the appointed season.

The emperor approved the proposal. From that time onward, the dì sacrifice was firmly established.

### The Greater Dì and the Lesser Dì <note>禘大禘小</note>

The Outer Commentary on the Rites states: "The dì sacrifice determines and establishes the order of seniority." <note>original: "禮外傳：禘，禘定"</note>

The greater dì and the lesser dì: the Spring and Autumn Annals records the dì but not the xiá. <note>This reflects a textual observation about which rites the Spring and Autumn Annals (春秋) chose to record.</note> Dismantled temples have no regular seasonal sacrifices; there are merely two grand sacrifices every five years. When a spirit tablet first enters the temple, a dì sacrifice is performed first. The following spring, a xiá is performed, and then another dì. Each year

### Combined Feast at the Grand Ancestor <note>合食太祖</note>

The Baihu Tongyi <note>White Tiger Hall Comprehensive Meanings, a Han dynasty compendium of ritual and doctrinal interpretations compiled under imperial patronage</note> states: "The dì sacrifice gathers the tablets from dismantled temples to share in the combined feast at the Grand Ancestor's temple."

According to the Comprehensive Meanings of the Five Classics <note>五經通義, a Han dynasty exegetical work</note>: when a king or feudal lord completes a three-year cycle, one intercalary month is inserted, and the heavenly way is thereby brought to a minor completion. Hence every three years there is a xiá sacrifice. The xiá gathers all tablets from temples not yet dismantled to share in the combined feast within the Grand Ancestor's temple. When five years have passed, two intercalary months have been inserted, and the heavenly way reaches a major completion. Hence every five years there is a dì sacrifice. The dì gathers the tablets already removed from their temples to share in the combined feast. This ensures that the ancestors are not forgotten in their essence, and that the line of succession is maintained from the near to the distant, never losing sight of the forebears.

It is also said: the dì sacrifice extends to those whose tablets have been transferred because they cannot continue to serve as rulers generation after generation. <note>This explains why the dì rite includes ancestors whose temples have been dismantled: since they can no longer receive individual worship through an unbroken line of descendants holding office, they are honored collectively in the grand sacrifice.</note>

Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the great Neo-Confucian commentator</note>, in the *Recorded Conversations*, was asked: "Is it the case that the Wang Feng is truly a Feng like the others, and was not demoted to the status of Guo Feng?" He replied: "One can see this from the language itself. Feng poetry mostly comes from those in lower positions, while Ya poetry is composed by scholar-officials. Although Ya poetry does contain satirical passages, its diction differs from that of Feng."

Master Chen Zhi <note>Chen Zhi, a Song-era scholar</note> said: Ya poems are mostly musical compositions for court assemblies and banquets, or works composed by dukes, ministers, and grand masters for the purpose of remonstrance and offering counsel. After the eastward move of the capital, the court no longer produced such compositions, and the ministers no longer offered such submissions, and so Ya poetry perished. Only the folk songs of the people remained.

# Collected Explanations of the Rites of Zhou, Volume 5

From this it may be seen that the palace suspension <note>gongxian: bells and chimes hung on all four sides, the privilege of the Son of Heaven</note> has four sides, and the gable suspension <note>xuanxian: hung on three sides, for feudal lords</note> has three sides; both are fully laid out with bells and chime-stones. Judging by the royal system, this is so; but judged by the system for feudal lords, it is again half of the royal system. When the king's ministers and grand masters have a split suspension, one array <term>si</term> <gloss>a full set of bells or chimes on its frame</gloss> on the east and one on the west, then the ministers and grand masters of the feudal lords have one wall <term>du</term> <gloss>a unit of hanging instruments, a half-array</gloss> east and west, as can be known. When the king's officers have a single suspension, one array on the south, then the officers of the feudal lords have one wall, as can be known.

# Book of Music, Juan 36

In harmony and compliance, none fail to be affectionate and close. Master Kong <note>the commentator Kong Yingda</note> said: The former kings wished to examine these through measures and numbers and to regulate them through rites and righteousness <note>original: 禮義</note>; without teaching this cannot be done, so they established schools of graded instruction. The ornamentation and pattern refers to the office and shang <note>gong and shang are notes of the five-tone scale</note> answering one another, like five colors forming a pattern. The former kings made music in order to transform the people: because the sounds of music were harmonious and regulated, the distinction between kin and strangers appears in music; because the sounds of music have clear and turbid, high and low, the distinction between noble and base, elder and younger appears in music; because the sounds of music have yin and yang, the pitch-pipes <note>lülü, the twelve standard pitches</note>, the principle of male and female appears in music.

The Master said: As for performance and ornamentation, the equalizing of sounds: the beginning is broad and the end restrained. The broadness of the beginning, the music cannot be made plain; the restraint of the ending in ornamentation must not be reduced. To guide by depth of virtue <note>original: 德厚</note> is to be able to make people return to the stillness of their nature and not chase the movement of things; how then could human desire exhaust and extinguish heavenly

<column-break/>

principle? He who follows the pitches records this; this assists this. The substance of music indeed has small and great; its use indeed has end and beginning. Recording by the correspondence of small and great, then small and great complete one another without inequality of weight; assisting with the order of end and beginning, then end and beginning beget one another without disorder of before and after. By this one images affairs and conduct: the character of affairs has small and great, end and beginning. Guiding by depth of virtue as one's nature, imaging affairs and conduct as one's conduct, then what is expressed in sound and formed in movement and stillness: one far, one near, and the principle of kin and strangers resides in it; one above, one below, and the principle of noble and base resides in it; one before, one after, and the principle of elder and younger resides in it; one within, one without, and the principle of male and female resides in it. Thus it can make these principles all take form in music. Does this not originate in the correspondence of small and great in the pitches?

頁二（續）

傳文中記載，戎人將要侵伐曹國。曹羈勸諫說：「戎人眾多而行事不義，請君上不要親自與他們為敵。」曹伯不肯聽從；曹羈諫了三次，仍不被採納，於是離開了曹國。

何休說：「勸諫有五種。第一是**諷諫**（間接勸諫），孔子即為一例。」

<gloss>按：定公十二年《公羊傳》記載，孔子因季氏日益強大，對季孫說：「卿大夫之家不可私藏甲兵，封邑不得超過百雉之城牆。」於是墮毀了費邑。</gloss>

第二是**順諫**（順勢勸諫），曹羈即為一例。

<gloss>按：此即前文曹羈勸諫曹伯之事。</gloss>

第三是**直諫**（直言勸諫），子家駒即為一例。

<gloss>按：昭公二十五年《公羊傳》記載，昭公論及天子之大夫（即季氏）時說，他們僭越諸侯之位已久。子家駒是不避諱君上之言而直言其僭越者。</gloss>

第四是**爭諫**（力爭勸諫），子反請求楚王撤軍即為一例。

<gloss>按：宣公十五年《公羊傳》記載，楚莊王圍攻宋國。宋國的華元與楚國的子反在城牆土壘間相對對話。華元對子反說：「宋人已到了交換兒子為食、拆解骸骨為炊的地步。」子反對華元說：「我軍只剩七日之糧。」子反勸說楚王撤兵歸國。</gloss>

<gloss>於是赦免宋國而退兵。子反屢屢強諫，楚王不聽，他便率領軍隊自行撤離，楚王也因此退兵歸國。</gloss>

第五是**戇諫**（愚直死諫）。

The Commentary states: The Rong were about to invade Cao. Cao Ji remonstrated, saying: "The Rong are numerous and act without righteousness. My lord, I beg you not to face them in battle yourself." The Earl of Cao would not agree. After three remonstrances went unheeded, Cao Ji departed.

He Xiu says there are five types of remonstrance:

The first is called <term>諷諫</term> <gloss>allusive remonstrance, using indirect suggestion rather than direct statement</gloss>. Confucius is an example of this. <gloss>According to the Gongyang Commentary for the twelfth year of Duke Ding, Confucius, having learned of the Ji clan's power, spoke forcefully to Ji Sun, saying: "A household should not store weapons of war; a walled town should not have walls a hundred雉 in circumference." He then brought about the dismantling of the walls of Bi.</gloss>

The second is called <term>順諫</term> <gloss>compliant remonstrance, gentle and deferential in tone</gloss>. Cao Ji is an example of this. <gloss>This refers to the remonstrance to the Earl of Cao described above.</gloss>

The third is called <term>直諫</term> <gloss>direct remonstrance, speaking frankly without circumlocution</gloss>. Zi Jiaju is an example of this. <gloss>According to the Gongyang Commentary for the twenty-fifth year of Duke Zhao, Duke Zhao said: "The great masters of the Son of Heaven have long been overstepping their rank relative to the feudal lords." This was speaking of usurpation without avoiding the ruler's own usurpation, stating it plainly.</gloss>

The fourth is called <term>爭諫</term> <gloss>contentious remonstrance, pressing urgently even at personal risk</gloss>. Zi Fan's request to withdraw is an example of this. <gloss>According to the Gongyang Commentary for the fifteenth year of Duke Xuan, King Zhuang of Chu besieged Song. Zi Fan of Chu and Hua Yuan of Song ascended opposite siege mounds and spoke to each other. Hua Yuan told Zi Fan: "We have been exchanging children to eat and splitting bones to use as fuel." Zi Fan told Hua Yuan: "Our army has only seven days of grain remaining." Zi Fan then urged the King of Chu to withdraw as well.</gloss>

The fifth is called <term>戇諫</term> <gloss>blunt remonstrance, persisting stubbornly even when ignored, regardless of consequence</gloss>. <gloss>After repeatedly remonstrating without being heeded, one led the troops away from Song and returned. The King of Chu also withdrew.</gloss>

# Book of Music, Volume 36

In harmony and accord, none fails to be harmonious and intimate. Master Kong <note>Kong Yingda, Tang-dynasty commentator</note> said: The former kings wished to examine music through measures and numbers, and to regulate it through ritual propriety. Since this could not be accomplished without teaching, they established schools and graded instruction. "Patterns and ornamentation" refers to how the <term>gong</term> <gloss>the first tone of the pentatonic scale</gloss> and <term>shang</term> <gloss>the second tone of the pentatonic scale</gloss> tones correspond to one another, just as the five colors combine to form a pattern. The former kings created music in order to transform the people. Because the sounds of music are modulated and harmonious, the distinctions of closeness and distance are made manifest in music. Because musical sounds possess clarity and turbidity, height and lowness, the distinctions of noble and base, elder and younger are made manifest in music. Because musical sounds possess <term>yin and yang</term> <gloss>the complementary cosmic forces</gloss> and the <term>lü and lü pitch pipes</term> <gloss>the twelve-tone system dividing yin and yang pitches</gloss>, the principles governing male and female are made manifest in music.

Master Chen said: When one performs the patterns and ornamentation, one adorns the balanced sounds. What begins broad must end in restraint; what begins broad in the manner of Changle <note>Chen Yang's home region, used here as a reference to his own scholarly tradition</note> must not be left without substance; what ends in restraint with patterns and ornamentation must not be left unexamined. When one uses these as a measuring-line for abundant virtue, one can cause people to return to the stillness of their original nature and not chase after the movements of external things. How then could there be any exhaustion of human desire or destruction of heavenly

<column-break/>

principle? The <term>lü pitch pipes</term> <gloss>the twelve-tone system</gloss> set forth this; this assists and supports this. The substance of music inherently possesses greatness and smallness; its function inherently possesses an end and a beginning. When one sets forth the appellation of greatness and smallness, then great and small complement each other and there is no inequality of weight. When one assists with the sequence of end and beginning, then end and beginning give rise to each other and there is no disorder of precedence. Through this one gives form to affairs and actions, and affairs may indeed possess greatness and smallness, end and beginning. When one uses abundant virtue as a measuring-line for nature, and gives form to affairs and actions as conduct, then the sounds of Yue <note>the ancient state of Yue, here representing music broadly</note> and the shapes of movement and stillness reveal: one far, one near, and the principle of closeness and distance is preserved; one above, one below, and the principle of noble and base is preserved; one preceding, one following, and the principle of elder and younger is preserved; one inner, one outer, and the principle of male and female is preserved. How is it that all these principles are made manifest in music? Does this not originate from the appellation of greatness and smallness in the pitch pipes?

The *yu* <note>敔， a percussion instrument stopped at the end of performances</note> is shaped like a lacquered tube with a contracted mouth, large at the top, two arms' circumference, five feet six inches long, covered with sheep hide, and having two loops. The "scattered painting" <note>疏畫， long sparse engraved lines</note> all follows Han models, from which we know this. It is said that Zheng's note on the *Jin Che* <note>巾車， "Carriages" chapter of the *Rites of Zhou*</note> gives the *zhu* <note>柷， an instrument struck to begin performances</note> a color of red with much black; the sparse lines are long, sparse, and engraved. Du Zichun reads *yuan* as the *di* of "cleansing" <note>蕩滌</note>, reading it as in the "Jiao Te Sheng" <note>郊特牲， chapter of the *Book of Rites*</note>: "when the savor and odor are not yet complete, it cleanses"; thus the sound's purity. What is now blown, the five-holed bamboo *sui*, comes after, and the Later Zheng follows him. It is further said that the *zhu* music is the music of the Xia. This is because the Bell Master <note>鍾師， an office in the *Rites of Zhou*</note> has *zhu* music; since this *zhu* music is the same, it is known that this *zhu* music being taught is the Xia *zhu* made by the Bell Master. It is said that since the Sheng Master <note>笙師， the office teaching wind instruments</note> teaches them, these three instruments in the courtyard can be known. Since they are known to be in the courtyard, the sheng pipes are below the hall; being near the hall, the three are likewise below the hall; being far from the hall, they are in the courtyard, as can be known.

<column-break/>

When it is time, they are blown. In winter water prevails <note>冬水用事， in the five-phases cycle winter belongs to water</note>; the number of water is six, and six times seven is forty-two; the length of the *yu* <note>竽， a mouth organ</note> is likely taken from this. The sheng has thirteen reeds. The *Guang Ya* says the sheng is made from a gourd, with thirteen pipes, the gong pipe on the left. The *yu* imitates it with thirty-six pipes, the gong pipe in the center. The *Tu on the Rites* says the *yu* is four feet two inches long; this *yu* with thirty-six reeds agrees with the *Tu on the Rites*. As for the *chi* <note>篪， a transverse bamboo flute</note> having seven holes: the *Guang Ya* says the *chi* is made of bamboo, one foot four inches long, with eight holes, one hole opening upward, one inch three tenths. The *Tu on the Rites* says the *chi* has nine holes. the Minister of Agriculture <note>司農， referring to Zheng Xing's commentary</note> says seven holes, which is likely a copyist's error; it should say eight holes. Or perhaps the Minister of Agriculture had a different source. It is said that the spring *du* <note>牘， a bamboo percussion instrument</note> is of bamboo, five or six inches thick, seven feet long, the shorter ones one or two feet, with two holes at its ends. Like the *zhu*, it is struck on the ground with both hands. The *ying* <note>應， a percussion instrument</note> is six feet five inches long and contains a clapper inside.

Zhang Nanxuan <note>Zhang Shi, Song dynasty scholar</note> said the tower took its name from the mountain: beside the present Yellow Crane Tower there is a mountain called Huanghu, "Yellow Swan." ## Yellow Crane Tower

Yellow Crane Tower is located in present-day Wuchang. The Tang dynasty gazetteer <note>唐圖經, a Tang-era geographical compendium</note> states that Fei Wenyi <note>費文禕, a legendary immortal</note> ascended to become an immortal, rode a yellow crane, and returned to rest at this place. Zhang Nanxuan <note>張南軒, i.e. Zhang Shi (1133–1180), a Southern Song Neo-Confucian scholar</note> said that Yellow Crane takes its name from the mountain, and today beside Yellow Crane Tower there is a mountain called Yellow Swan. Nanxuan's explanation is correct.

Examining the character 鵠 (swan): Cai Heng <note>蔡衡, a Han-dynasty commentator</note> said that among phoenixes those that are mostly white in colour are called 鵠. The *Suoyin* commentary <note>索隱, Sima Zhen's commentary on the Shiji</note> says that 鴻鵠 is a single bird, resembling the phoenix. Thus the swan belongs to the phoenix category. Some call it 鴻 (great wild goose), some call it white, some call it yellow, and that is all. Yellow and white are close in colour. 鴻 means "great." The commentary to the *Siqiu* section <note>司裘, an office in the Zhouli (Rites of Zhou)</note> says that 鵠 refers to wild geese; the swan is a small bird that is difficult to hit. The *Yupian* dictionary <note>玉篇, a sixth-century character dictionary by Gu Yewang</note> states: "鴈鵠 is the same as 鵠; it is a bird that knows the future." It is covered with sheepskin, and has two knobs. The widely spaced painted patterns are all described with reference to Han dynasty practice. The Zheng commentary on the <term>Jin Che</term> <gloss>"Chariots and Drapery" chapter</gloss> states: the <term>zhu</term> <gloss>a box-shaped percussion instrument struck to begin music</gloss> is colored with much red and little black. "Widely spaced painted patterns" means the lines are drawn far apart. Zi Chun reads the character <term>yuan</term> <gloss>distant</gloss> as the <term>di</term> <gloss>to cleanse</gloss> of "cleansing and purifying," and reads it following the phrase from the <term>Jiao Te Sheng</term> <gloss>"Single Victim at the Suburban Sacrifice" chapter of the Liji</gloss>: "the fragrant tastes are not yet complete, cleansing and purifying their sound." He says that what is blown today is the five-holed bamboo pipe. Later Zheng followed this reading. "Established" refers to the <term>zhu</term> music. That the <term>zhu</term> is the music of the <term>Zhu</term> <gloss>referring to the Xia dynasty style</gloss> is because the Bell Master has <term>zhu</term> music, and this <term>zhu</term> music corresponds to it. Therefore we know that the <term>zhu</term> music taught here is the <term>zhu xia</term> <gloss>zhu-style summer music</gloss> performed by the Bell Master. The text says the Sheng Master teaches it, so that the three instruments are placed in the courtyard. This can be known.

<column-break/>

At the time of the winter solstice it is blown. In winter, water is the operative element; the number of water is six. Six times seven gives forty-two. The length of the <term>yu</term> <gloss>a large mouth-organ with 36 pipes</gloss> is presumably derived from this. The <term>sheng</term> <gloss>a mouth-organ</gloss> has thirteen reeds. The <term>Guang Ya</term> <gloss>"Expanded Elegant Words," a dictionary</gloss> says: the <term>sheng</term> is made from a gourd, with thirteen pipes; the <term>gong</term> <gloss>the fundamental tone</gloss> pipe is on the left side. The <term>yu</term> resembles it but has thirty-six pipes; the <term>gong</term> pipe is in the center. The <term>Li Tu</term> <gloss>"Illustrations of the Rites," a Han-era illustrated ritual manual</gloss> says: the <term>yu</term> is four <term>chi</term> and two <term>cun</term> long. This <term>yu</term> with thirty-six reeds agrees with the <term>Li Tu</term>. The text says the <term>chi</term> <gloss>a transverse flute</gloss> has seven holes. The <term>Guang Ya</term> says: the <term>chi</term> is made of bamboo, one <term>chi</term> and four <term>cun</term> long, with eight holes; one hole projects upward by one <term>cun</term> and three <term>fen</term> <gloss>one-tenth of a cun</gloss>. The <term>Li Tu</term> says: the <term>chi</term> has nine holes. Si Nong <gloss>Zheng Zhong, a Han commentator</gloss> says seven holes. This is probably a scribal error; it should say eight holes. Or perhaps Si Nong had a different source. The <term>ying</term> <gloss>a small drum or percussion instrument used to respond to the zhu</gloss> is six <term>chi</term> and five <term>cun</term> long, and has a mallet inside it.

# Monthly Sacrifices, the La Sacrifice, and the Hundred Spirits

At the *Laba* <note>La sacrifice, year-end sacrifice</note>, offerings are made to the Hundred Spirits.

At the **Beginning of Spring**, sacrifice at the Eastern Supreme Unity Palace. At the **Beginning of Summer** and **Beginning of Winter**, sacrifice at the Central Supreme Unity Palace. At the **Beginning of Autumn**, sacrifice at the Western Supreme Unity Palace.

## Middle-Grade Sacrifices: Fourteen in All

- After the Beginning of Spring, on a *hai* day, sacrifice to the First Farmer <term>xian nong</term>.
- Twenty days after the Beginning of Spring, sacrifice to the Master of Winds <term>feng shi</term>.
- In mid-spring, sacrifice to the Five Dragons <term>wu long</term>.
- In late spring, make offering to the First Silkworm <term>xian can</term>.
- After the Beginning of Summer, on a *shen* day, sacrifice to the Masters of Rain and Masters of Thunder.
- On the *si* and *li* days <note>the four "standing" season days, and the days when earth attains kingship at the end of each season</note>, sacrifice to the Mountains and Peaks, Seas and Rivers.
- On the first *wu* day of mid-spring and mid-autumn, perform the Foundation Offering <term>shidian</term> <gloss>school sacrifice to Confucius</gloss> for King Wucheng <note>a posthumous title honoring Jiang Ziya, the ancient strategist</note>.

## Lesser Sacrifices: Thirteen in All

- After the Beginning of Winter, on a *hai* day, sacrifice to the Directors of the Center, of Fate, of the People, and of Emolument.
- At the autumn equinox, offer to the Longevity Star.
- After the Beginning of Autumn, on a *chen* day, sacrifice to the_numinous Star <term>ling xing</term>.
- At the start of winter, sacrifice to the Director of Cold <note>the Water God</note>.
- In mid-spring, sacrifice to the Ancestor of Horses; in mid-summer, make offering to the First Herdsman; in mid-autumn, sacrifice to the Altar of Horses; in mid-winter, sacrifice at the Horse Steps.
- At the Beginning of Spring, sacrifice to the Household Director of Fate <note>the hearth-god of the household gates and fates</note>.
- At the Beginning of Summer, sacrifice to the Hearth <term>zao</term>.
- In late summer, on the earth-kingship day, sacrifice at the Center Beam <term>zhong liu</term> <gloss>the house's central point</gloss>.
- At the Beginning of Autumn, sacrifice at the Gates and to the Wandering Souls <note>malevolent spirits without descendants</note>.
- At the Beginning of Winter, sacrifice at the Great... <unclear>祠</unclear> [text continues beyond page].

The dances of the Tang dynasty, namely the Anle (Peace and Joy), Taiping (Great Peace), Pozhen (Breaking the Battle Line), Qingshan (Celebration of Goodness), Dading (Great Stabilization), Shangyuan (Upper Origin), Shengshou (Sagely Longevity), and Guangsheng (Glorious Sageliness) dances, were all accompanied by great drums mixed with the music of <term>Qiuci</term> <gloss>Kucha, a Central Asian kingdom whose music heavily influenced Tang court music</gloss>. The Dading dance added the gong of metal. Only the Qingshan dance alone used the music of Xiliang <note>Western Liang, another Central Asian musical tradition</note>. Formerly, the three dances of Pozhen, Shangyuan, and Qingshan were all given changed robes and caps, combined with bells and chimestones, and performed separately at the suburban and ancestral temple sacrifices. The Pozhen dance served as the martial dance of the Seven Virtues <note>commemorating the military achievements of Emperor Taizong</note>, and the Qingshan dance as the civil dance of the Nine Merits. After Empress Wu usurped power and destroyed the ancestral temples of the Tang, this rite came to an end. The eight dances including Anle were all performed standing, and the Court of Imperial Sacrifices called them the standing-division performers <term>libu ji</term> <gloss>standing-division entertainers</gloss>. The *Calendar Treatise* <note>original: 歷志， the treatise on calendrical science in the Han History</note> says: Huangzhong <term>黃鐘</term> <gloss>Yellow Bell, the first of the twelve pitches</gloss> is the norm of Heaven, its pitch-pipe nine cun long; Linzhong <term>林鐘</term> <gloss>Forest Bell</gloss> is the norm of Earth, its pitch-pipe six cun long; Dazu <term>大族</term> <gloss>Great Seedling, also written 大呂</gloss> is the norm of Man, its pitch-pipe eight cun long. It further says that the twelve pipes generate one another, always advancing by eight positions, rising and falling, until the generation is complete at the central lü <note>original: 生盡於中呂</note>. Yin and yang arise from Huangzhong, beginning with a leftward rotation. "Eight by eight as position" means this: for example, Huangzhong generates Linzhong, which is an advance of eight stations; everything below this follows the same rule, hence "eight by eight as position."

# The *Discourses of the States*: pitch-pipes are what establish the equal temperament

## "And determine the measures. The ancient blind music-masters of the spirits examined the mean sounds and measured by them to fix the pitch-pipes and equal-temper the bells," it says.

### Using the mean sounds to fix the pitches, and the pitches to establish the equal temperament of the bells.

The Jia commentary <note>original: 賈疏， the subcommentary of Jia Gongyan</note> quotes the *Discourses of the States* <term>國語</term> <gloss>Discourses of the States</gloss> because it wishes to take the principle that great and small must accord with the same pitches. "Mean sounds" refers to the upward and downward generation, the lengths that fix the pitches. "Measuring the pitches" means reckoning by the pitches themselves, from the doubled and halved values, and thereby establishing the equal temperament of the bells, which is precisely according with the lengths of the pitches. According to the original meaning in the *Discourses of the States*: "examining the mean sounds" means using them to make the pipe of Huangzhong; "measuring them" means carefully scrutinizing the full measure of the mean sounds; "measuring the pitches" means that once the dimensions of Huangzhong are obtained, one thereby measures the fractions of upward and downward generation to determine the short and long of the twelve pitch-pipes; "equal-tempering the bells" means that on the basis of the pitch-pipes one establishes the temperament and tunes the sounds of the two sets of bells through the twelve pitches.

The Tang dynasty dances including Anle, Taiping, Pozhen, Qingshan, Dading, Shangyuan, Shengshou, and Guangsheng all employed large drums mixed with the music of Kucha <note>original: 龜茲, a Central Asian oasis kingdom whose musical traditions profoundly influenced Tang court music</note>. The Dading music additionally incorporated bronze gongs. Only the Qingshan Dance uniquely used Western Liang <note>a region in present-day Gansu, whose music represented a blend of Chinese and Central Asian traditions</note> music alone. Formerly, the three dances of Pozhen, Shangyuan, and Qingshan had their costumes altered and were combined with bells and stone chimes for separate offerings at the suburban temples. Pozhen was designated the Martial Dance of the Seven Virtues <note>referring to the seven military virtues attributed to Emperor Taizong</note>, and Qingshan was designated the Civil Dance of the Nine Merits <note>referring to nine civil accomplishments</note>. After Empress Wu <note>Wu Zetian, who usurped the Tang throne and established her own Zhou dynasty</note> seized power and destroyed the Tang ancestral temples, these rites were entirely abolished. The Anle and the other eight dances were all performed standing; the Music Bureau called them the Standing Division <note>original: 立部伎, performers who danced while standing, as opposed to the Seated Division who performed while seated</note>. # The <term>Guoyu</term> <gloss>Discourses of the States</gloss> on How Pitch Pipes Establish Tuning

## Measures and Standards of Emergence; the Blind Musicians of Antiquity Examined the Central Tones and Measured Them to Establish the Pitch Pipes, Tuning Standards, and Bells

### Establishing Pitch Pipes from the Central Tones, and Establishing the Tuning of Bells from the Pitch Pipes

<term>Jia Gongyan's</term> <gloss>Tang dynasty subcommentator</gloss> subcommentary cites the <term>Guoyu</term> <gloss>Discourses of the States</gloss> because he wishes to draw upon the correspondence between the sizes of bells and the pitch pipes. The "central tones" refer to the tones generated above and below, which determine the lengths of the pitch pipes. To "measure the pipes" means to calculate by means of the pipes, proceeding from doubling and halving to establish the tuning of the bells. This is precisely what corresponds to the lengths of the pipes. Examining the original meaning of the <term>Guoyu</term> passage: "examining the central tones" means using them to fashion the Huangzhong pipe. "Measuring them" means scrutinizing the balanced quantities of the central tones. "Measuring the pipes" means: having obtained the numerical values of Huangzhong, one proceeds to measure the fractional amounts of its upward and downward generation, thereby determining the short and long of the twelve pitch pipes. "Tuning the bells" means: using the pitch pipes to establish the tuning standard, so as to regulate the sounds of the twelve pipes and the two bells <note>referring to the large and small bells used in court music</note>.
